As for their words 'we used to call upon Him before', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as worship, supplication and humility, whereas Ibn al-Qayyim sees a call of worship that includes a request, and holds that salvation comes through sincere worship rather than mere asking. On the divine name al-Barr, Ibn Abbas explains it as the Subtle One, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak as the Truthful in His promise, and others as the Bountiful Benefactor. The readings differ: Nafi and al-Kisa'i read 'annahu' with a fatha, meaning 'because He', while the rest read 'innahu' with a kasra, starting a new sentence; al-Tabari judges both readings valid. Ibn Kathir also reports that Aisha used to recite this verse while pleading with Allah.

This passage records what the people of Paradise say to one another: they recall that in the world, among their families, they lived in fear and anxiety of their Lord's punishment, but Allah bestowed His favour on them and protected them from the punishment of the samum, which most commentators take to be the fire of Hell and its scorching heat that penetrates the pores. They add that they used to call upon Him before, that is, worship Him sincerely and ask Him for salvation, and then they give the reason: indeed He is the Righteous, the Merciful. Ibn Abbas explains al-Barr as the Gentle, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij as the one who keeps His promise, and al-Khattabi as the one whose goodness embraces all His creatures. Most commentators say al-Rahim is the one of abundant mercy, who rewards those who worship Him and answers those who ask Him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the word da'wa may mean worship or petition, and both meanings are included; Ibn al-Qayyim argues that salvation is gained through sincere worship rather than mere asking. The readings differ on the word annahu: Nafi, al-Kisai and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha, meaning 'because He is', while the other readers use a kasra and begin a new clause; al-Tabari holds that both readings are valid. The verse contains no legal ruling and no disputed juristic point; it describes the state of the believers in Paradise and gives the reason for their deliverance.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to keep reminding people through the Qur'an, and clears him of the charges of soothsaying and madness that the polytheists hurled at him. The commentators explain that the blessing of God upon him, namely the soundness of his mind and the truth of his prophethood, keeps him from these things. A kahin, they say, is one who announces hidden matters with the help of a jinn, and a majnun is one whose reason has been disturbed. Most link the verse to the words of 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and to the meeting of Quraysh at Dar al-Nadwa, where someone said he was a poet whose death they should await, as had happened to Zuhayr and Nabigha. As for 'rayb al-manun', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean death, while Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean the calamities of time, and some identify al-Manun with time itself. The exegetes generally read 'Wait, and I am with you among those who wait' as a threat. They differ on the particle 'am', which some render as 'bal' and others as a question, and Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as a rebuke: their reason does not command such a claim. The passage also leads into the challenge to produce a discourse like the Qur'an.

The commentators explain that God commands His Prophet ﷺ to keep reminding people with the Quran and clears him of the charges of soothsaying and madness made by the polytheists. The verse then reports their claim that he is a poet, whom they await to be struck by the misfortunes of time until he dies as the poets before him did. All agree that the word tarabbus means simply waiting. On the phrase rayb al-manun, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Ishaq, and al-Tabari in his main view, take it to mean death, while Mujahid, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean the calamities of fate. Some say that manun denotes both time and death, citing the line of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that the remark was made when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwa. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the particle am here marks a shift in speech, with an admonishing question. According to al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur, God's reply, "Wait, then; I am waiting with you," is a threat, and the Prophet himself awaits their downfall or the failure of their scheme.

In this verse God commands His Messenger ﷺ to answer those who called him a poet and said they were waiting for him to be struck by the vicissitudes of fate. He tells them to wait, for he too is waiting along with them. The commentators agree that the imperative is a threat and a challenge rather than a permission. The most common reading is that the idolaters hoped for the Prophet's death, as had happened to other poets, and he replies that he is waiting for their ruin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that rayb al-manun means death, citing Ibn Abbas, while Mujahid explains it as the misfortunes of time; most exegetes combine both meanings. Al-Razi suggests several readings: the Prophet's waiting may be for the punishment that will overtake them, or for the lasting of his message after his death. Ibn Ashur links the threat to the battle of Badr and notes that the Prophet waits together with the believers. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan explain that the particle am here introduces a question of denial or a shift to another matter, depending on the opinion. The commentators draw no legal ruling from this verse and mostly see in it a warning to the disbelievers.

In this verse God affirms that the reason of the disbelievers does not command them to say what they say about the Prophet ﷺ, since the descriptions of soothsayer, poet and madman are contradictory and cannot be combined in one person. The commentators explain that "dreams" here means intellects, and that attributing the command to them is a metaphor meaning that they lead to it. For most of them, the implied answer is that they are a rebellious people who exceed all bounds in obstinacy although the truth has become clear to them: it is rebellion, not reason, that drove them to these claims. Al-Tabari and Mujahid take "am" to mean "bal" (rather), al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba read it as an interrogative, while Ibn 'Atiyya links it both to "bal" and to the interrogative. Ibn 'Ashur reads an interrogative of reproach blaming their loss of discernment. The verse belongs to the flow of the surah: after the command to the Prophet to remind, and the denial that he is a soothsayer or a madman, the commentators report that some Quraysh, gathered in Dar al-Nadwa, had said he was a poet and that they should wait for his death, and God answers by ordering the Prophet to tell them to wait, since he too is waiting. The word "tughyan" is explained as transgressing limits in opposition. Some, such as al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin, stress that some of them inwardly knew the truth but pride led them to deny it. The commentators largely agree on the meaning and differ mainly on how to read the particle "am" and on the scope of the word "ahlam".

The commentators explain that the verse reports the claim of the polytheists that the Qur'an is the Prophet's own fabrication, something he invented of his own accord. Most of them place the answer in the words "Nay, they do not believe": their rejection stems from disbelief and obstinacy rather than from any lack of evidence, since they know their accusation is false, as al-Nasafi and al-Qasimi note. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take "they do not believe" to mean that they refuse to accept the truth sent by their Lord, while al-Baghawi explains taqawwul as forcing speech, a term used only for lying, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya describe it as a specific kind of falsehood. On the particle "am", Mujahid and Abu 'Ubayda take it to mean "bal" with a question, whereas al-Zajjaj treats it as a rhetorical interrogation, and al-Khalil, as Ibn Kathir reports, holds that the whole series of such "am" in the surah is interrogative rather than conjunctive. In the challenge to "produce a discourse like it", al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya specify that the likeness required is in arrangement, eloquence and conciseness. Al-Razi reports that most Sunnis ground the inimitability in its eloquence, while others attribute it to God turning people away from imitating it; the advocates of the sarfa theory held that the Arabs could have done so but were prevented, whereas the majority say they never could, according to Ibn 'Atiyya. Some readers wrote "bi-hadith mithlihi" without tanwin, meaning "like the Messenger", as al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note.

In this verse God challenges the disbelievers to produce a discourse like the Qur'an, if they are truthful in their claim that Muhammad fabricated it. The commentators explain that the verse answers the accusation that the Prophet invented the Qur'an, since taqawwul usually means a deliberate fabrication. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the demand as bringing a text similar to it, noting that the disbelievers share the Prophet's language and would therefore be able to do so if they were sincere. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi specify that the expected likeness concerns composition, arrangement and conciseness, and al-Razi regards the imperative as a challenge meant to expose inability rather than a real command. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi report that the reading of al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal, with the genitive construction, means a discourse by a man like the Messenger, who was unlettered and had not studied with scholars. On whether the Arabs could have produced such a text before Islam, Ibn 'Atiyya reports the majority opinion that they never could, and the view of a minority who speak of a divine turning away (sarfa). Ibn 'Ashur sees the word hadith as meaning speech in general, or accounts similar to the stories of the Qur'an. Al-Shinqiti notes that the challenge recurs in several surahs, from al-Baqara to al-Isra'.

In this verse God asks the idolaters a rhetorical question that rules out two possibilities at once: were they created from nothing, that is without a creator, or did they create themselves? Most commentators conclude that both are impossible, so a Creator must exist, and He alone deserves worship. Al-Tabari explains that "from nothing" means they would be like lifeless objects that neither understand nor obey, and he also reports the view that they were created purposelessly. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi follow this reading and stress that the first question denies they came into being without a creator. Ibn al-Qayyim develops the argument with the example of a building, which implies a builder, and notes that no one can create himself. Al-Samani, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi offer further senses: some take it as "for nothing", meaning without aim or reward, others as "not from dust or water". Al-Razi holds that the first denial is the more obvious of the two. Al-Qurtubi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi also read the question as a rejection of self-creation. The hadith in al-Bukhari, in which Jubayr ibn Mut'im says his heart almost flew when he heard this surah, is cited by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin, while Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi focus on the logic of creation as proof of God's oneness.

This verse confronts the polytheists with a series of rhetorical questions: were they created from nothing, are they the creators of themselves, or did they create the heavens and the earth? Al-Tabari reads the answer as no, they did not create the heavens and the earth, and their lack of certainty about God's threat and punishment in the hereafter is what drives them to disobey. Ibn Kathir sees the passage as affirming God's lordship and oneness, and argues that their lack of certainty leads them to associate partners with God even though they acknowledge that He alone is the Creator. Al-Samani, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that these people admitted God created the heavens and the earth, so the argument turns against them. Al-Razi explains that the three questions form a progression, and that the creation of man from a drop of semen proves both divine unity and resurrection. He notes several possible meanings of 'from nothing': without a creator, purposelessly, or without a father and mother. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that dividing the possibilities into three reaches the conclusion of a single Creator by the shortest route. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the questions as rhetorical rebukes. The commentators agree on the general sense of condemning polytheism and affirming God's oneness, and differ on how to read 'from nothing' and on what kind of certainty is lacking.

In this verse God rebukes the disbelievers with a series of questions: do they possess the treasuries of your Lord, so that they give to whom they wish and withhold from whom they wish, or are they the dominant masters who run affairs as they please? Ibn Abbas explained the word al-musaytirun as those who hold power, and al-Tabari also reports from him the sense of those who send down, while Abu Ubayda, Ata and Mu'ammar ibn al-Muthanna took it to mean lords and overlords. Al-Tabari prefers the meaning of arrogant tyrants who rise up against God, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several meanings, including the guardians who record. The verse then asks whether they have a ladder by which they climb to listen in on the heavens; if they claim so, let their listener bring a clear proof. Al-Razi notes that denying the listening is stronger than denying the ascent, and he discusses how the preposition can mean on or in. Ibn Kathir reports that Jubayr ibn Mut'im heard this surah while still a polytheist, and that it was among the things that led him to Islam. The commentators agree on the general point that power and knowledge of the unseen belong to God alone, though they differ on the exact sense of several terms.

In this verse God puts a rhetorical question to the polytheists: do they have a ladder by which they ascend to heaven and listen there to the revelation and to what is said in the higher realm, so that they know their belief is true? He then challenges them to produce someone who claims to have listened, with a clear proof of his claim. Al-Tabari understands the word sulam as a means, a rung or a step by which one reaches something, and most commentators such as al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take it as a literal ladder to the sky; Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi confirm this concrete meaning and cite verses of Arabic poetry. As for the phrase yastami'una fihi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as listening while ascending, whereas al-Wahidi, reported by al-Razi, takes fi to mean upon, and Abu Hayyan notes that prepositions may replace one another. Opinions differ on what is heard: the revelation according to al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, what God decrees according to Ibn Kathir, or the claims made against the Prophet according to al-Razi. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur see in the verse an ironic way of denying that they have any knowledge of the unseen. Several commentators, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, treat it as one more argument in the chain of proofs in the surah, before the following verse turns to the daughters attributed to God.

God asks the polytheists of Quraysh, in a tone of rebuke and mockery, whether He would have daughters while they have sons. They attributed female angels to God while reserving males for themselves and despising daughters. The commentators agree that the verse denounces this claim and ridicules their reasoning, which the Quran elsewhere calls an unjust division. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress the reproachful character of the question, part of a series of rhetorical questions in this passage. Al-Razi reads it as an indirect proof that God has no associate or offspring: procreation is needed only by a mortal being, whereas God is living and self-subsisting. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the argument is framed in a way that persuades minds unable to grasp a purely logical demonstration, since males were regarded as superior to females. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Shinqiti point to parallel verses to complete the meaning. All the commentators cited reject the belief as false, and the discussion concerns mainly how best to refute it, with no particular legal consequence.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ in a tone of rebuke: does he ask these people for a fee for delivering the message, so that the burden of payment makes them shun Islam? The commentators agree that the meaning is a denial that he asked them for anything. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain that a demanded reward would weigh so heavily on them that they could not embrace Islam. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take the word maghram to mean a financial charge one takes on without being obliged to, which makes them reluctant to follow him. Al-Zamakhshari defines it the same way. Ibn 'Ashur sees a mocking remark that removes the reasons for their rejection, since merely being asked would already be embarrassing. Al-Razi concludes that the Prophet demanded nothing, and links this to the reward mentioned in al-Shura. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani give the same reading. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the Prophet spent his own wealth to win hearts, and mentions that some scholars derive from the verse a prohibition on charging for teaching knowledge, a view he considers open to question.

This verse poses a rhetorical question of rejection to the idolaters who claimed to possess knowledge of the unseen. The commentators generally read it as asking whether they have knowledge of the unseen so that they could write it down and report it to people, and the implied answer is no, since only God knows the unseen. The meaning of writing is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas took it to refer to the Preserved Tablet, from which they would copy and announce its contents. Qatada and Ibn Qutayba understood it as judging or decreeing, and Ibn 'Atiyya explained that they would prescribe for people the worship of idols and the practice of sawa'ib. Qatada linked the verse to the Quraysh's wish for the Prophet's death, and others read it as knowing when he would die. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that writing may signify a firm, unchangeable affirmation, or a literal recording of knowledge. Ibn Kathir reports that Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who heard these verses, was among the factors that led him to Islam. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the Prophet himself knew only what God revealed to him of the unseen.

This verse answers the polytheists' schemes and states that their plot against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers will fall back on themselves. Al-Tabari explains that they intend a plot against you and the religion of God, but they are the ones who will be outwitted; so trust in God and carry on with what He commanded you. The commentators agree that the reference is to the Quraysh plot in the Dar al-Nadwa, to imprison, kill or expel the Prophet. Al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that this scheme turned against them when they were killed at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take 'those who disbelieved' to mean the Quraysh, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud allow that it may include every disbeliever. Al-Razi lists several meanings of 'kayd': the whisperings of Satan, or God's punishment, and notes that the indefinite noun suggests a punishment that comes suddenly. Ibn 'Ashur sees a clear threat in the verse. The overall meaning is that the plotting of the disbelievers recoils upon them, and victory belongs to the Prophet and the believers.

The verse asks whether the disbelievers have any deity other than God, and then declares God exalted above what they associate with Him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy read the question as a denial: there is no other god who could protect them from God's punishment or provide for them and help them, and they conclude that no such god exists. Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di see it as a sharp rejection of idolatry, while al-Jaza'iri and the Tafsir al-Muyassar present it as the closing point of the surah's refutation of the disbelievers.

The commentators agree that the answer is negative and that the verse ends by glorifying God above their partners. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan describe the question as a rhetorical rebuke, and Ibn 'Ashur calls it the final and strongest blow against their polytheism, which he regards as the most comprehensive of errors. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that these idols are false gods in reality, though the idolaters claimed them as gods.

Al-Sam'ani raises a question: since the disbelievers did claim other gods, how can the verse ask whether they have one? He answers that these gods had no power to give life or death, provision or deprivation, so they are not gods in the true sense. Al-Razi observes that the verse restates the affirmation of God's oneness after the mention of daughters attributed to Him.

They differ on the grammar of "what they associate with Him". Al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi allow that "ma" may be a verbal noun, meaning God is exalted above their association, or a relative pronoun, meaning above what they associate with Him, which could be the claim of daughters or the idols themselves.

This passage describes the obstinacy of the Meccan disbelievers, who demanded that a piece of the sky fall upon them as punishment. God says that even if they saw it happen, they would not believe, but would say it is merely a heap of clouds. The commentators agree that kisf means a fragment, and that the deniers, out of pride and stubbornness, reject plain evidence. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi compare this verse to the passage in Surat al-Hijr about the gates of heaven. The text then tells the Prophet to leave them until the day they are struck down. Al-Tabari and others take this as the day of the first blast, Qatada as the day of their death, and Ibn Kathir as the Day of Resurrection. Readings of yuṣ'aqūna differ, and al-Tabari prefers the open form as more eloquent, while accepting the other. As for the lesser punishment, opinions vary: Ibn Abbas and al-Bara' ibn Azib say it is the punishment of the grave, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil the killing at Badr, Mujahid famine for seven years, and al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd the calamities of this world. The patience asked of the Prophet is linked by commentators to persisting in his mission, and 'you are under Our eyes' means protection and watchfulness. Finally, the glorification upon rising is interpreted in several ways: on leaving a gathering, on waking, on standing for prayer, or as the dawn prayer, with no single view clearly preferred.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to leave the disbelievers alone until they meet the day in which they will be struck senseless, that is, die or be destroyed. The commentators differ on which day this is. Qatada, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take it to be the Day of Resurrection, when terror will overcome them. Qatada in another report and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to be the day of their death. Ibn Abbas and others say it is the day of Badr, when they were punished. Al-Mawardi explains that sa'q means fainting. The preceding verse shows that even if they saw a piece of the sky falling on them, they would call it a heap of clouds, which reveals their obstinacy. Several exegetes read the command as a threat rather than an instruction. Some, such as al-Nahhas, said the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, but Ibn al-Jawzi considered this abrogation unsound, since the verse is a warning. Most say that the wrongdoers will suffer a lesser punishment in this world before the Last Day. They offer several explanations: the punishment of the grave according to al-Bara' and Ibn Abbas in one report, the killing at Badr according to Ibn Abbas and others, the seven years of famine according to Mujahid, and afflictions according to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Qayyim considers the warning to cover both this world and the intermediate state of the barzakh.

This verse states that on the Day when the wrongdoers are struck down, their schemes will not avail them at all, and no one will come to their aid. Al-Tabari explains that the kayd here refers to their plotting, and that no helper will exact retribution from those who punished them. Ibn Kathir stresses that the scheming they practised in this world will be of no benefit on that Day. Al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud take the scheming to mean their plots against the Prophet, while Ibn 'Ashur reads the phrase as meaning that they will have no scheming left to rely on at all. Al-Razi, who discusses the grammar at length, says that the words "nor will they be helped" complete the thought: a person in trouble first tries to save himself, then seeks the support of others, and neither will serve them.

The commentators agree that the punishment "short of that Day" falls on the wrongdoers in this life, but they differ on its nature. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and others say it is the punishment of the grave, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Ibn Zayd and al-Qurtubi point to the killing at Badr. Mujahid mentions the famine of seven years, and al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd the afflictions suffered in wealth and children. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse embraces all these forms together, whereas Ibn al-Qayyim holds that it may refer both to worldly punishment and to the punishment of the barzakh.

As for the verb "yusa'qun", it is read in different ways in terms of vowels, and the exegetes explain it as meaning either to die or to be struck senseless by terror.

This part of the verse declares that God has prepared for those who wronged themselves, through disbelief and the association of partners with Him, a punishment before the Day of Judgment, and that most of them do not realise it. The commentators agree that the 'wrongdoers' here are the stubborn disbelievers of Makkah, and that this punishment is in this world rather than in the Hereafter. They differ on its exact form. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and in one report Ibn 'Abbas, understood it as the punishment of the grave, and Ibn 'Abbas also linked it to the killing at Badr, a view shared by Muqatil and al-Tabari. Mujahid and al-Dahhak named the seven years of famine that struck Quraysh, while al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd took it to mean worldly afflictions such as the loss of wealth and children, illness and hardship. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir combined these readings, holding that the warning covers punishment in this life, including defeat and calamity, as well as the punishment of the intermediate state in the grave. Al-Tabari judged the wording general, with no single type of punishment singled out. Ibn Mas'ud's reading was 'beneath that, nearby'. Most of the commentators explain that the people's ignorance is the reason they fail to heed the warning.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to be patient with the judgment of his Lord, meaning what He decrees and prescribes, including the delay in answering the disbelievers and the hardship of conveying the message, and assures him that he is under God's watchful eye and protection. He is then commanded to glorify and praise his Lord at certain times. The commentators agree on the meaning of protection and support, but differ on the times intended. Abu al-Ahwas, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Thawri understood it as the phrase said on rising from a gathering, which expiates what was said there, as narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and others took it as rising from sleep, al-Kalbi as remembrance from bed until entering prayer, while al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' took it as the opening supplication of prayer. As for part of the night and the fading of the stars, most, including Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority, understood the two units of prayer before dawn, while al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd understood the dawn prayer, and Muqatil the evening and night prayers. Some considered the command to patience abrogated by the verse of the sword, which Ibn al-Jawzi rejects, and al-Tabari took the command as a recommendation rather than an obligation where no proof of obligation exists.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to glorify his Lord with praise at several times. The commentators explain "and for part of the night, glorify Him" as prayer or remembrance during part of the night, and "and at the retreat of the stars" as the time when the stars fade at dawn. Most exegetes agree that glorification here means prayer and that the retreat of the stars is the time of the dawn prayer. Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, Jabir and Anas take it to mean the two units of prayer before dawn, while al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the obligatory dawn prayer. Al-Tabari prefers the obligatory prayer, since a command implies obligation unless proof shows otherwise. As for the part of the night, Ibn Zayd and others identify it with the night prayer, al-Baghawi and Muqatil include the maghrib and 'isha' prayers, and Mujahid understands it as the whole night. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others cite 'A'isha's report that the Prophet was most consistent with the two units before dawn, some seeing a recommendation there and others an abrogation by the five daily prayers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi note that glorifying during part of the night is harder on the soul and further from showing off.
